claims.quote: Up to 50 certificates can be issued per registered domain (or IPv4 address, or IPv6 /64 range) every 7 days.
claims.claim: The limit for new certificates per registered domain is 50 every 7 days.

claims.quote: The ability to issue new certificates for the same registered domain refills at a rate of 1 certificate every 202 minutes.
claims.claim: The refill rate for this limit is 1 certificate every 202 minutes.

claims.quote: A registered domain is, generally speaking, the part of the domain you purchased from your domain name registrar. For instance, in www.example.com, the registered domain is example.com. In new.blog.example.co.uk, the registered domain is example.co.uk.
claims.claim: The definition of a registered domain is determined by the Public Suffix List, typically corresponding to the portion purchased from a registrar.

claims.quote: Renewals are treated specially: they don't count against your Certificates per Registered Domain limit, but they are subject to a Duplicate Certificate limit of 5 per week.
claims.claim: Renewals are exempt from the main domain limit but are subject to a separate duplicate limit of 5 per week.

claims.quote: A certificate is considered a renewal (or a duplicate) of an earlier certificate if it contains the exact same set of hostnames, ignoring capitalization and ordering of hostnames.
claims.claim: A duplicate is defined as a certificate with the exact same set of hostnames, regardless of order or capitalization.

claims.quote: Exceeding the Duplicate Certificate limit is reported with the error message too many certificates already issued for exact set of domains.
claims.claim: The specific error message for hitting the duplicate limit is "too many certificates already issued for exact set of domains".

claims.quote: Up to 5 authorization failures per identifier can be incurred by one account every hour.
claims.claim: The limit for authorization failures is 5 per identifier per account every hour.

claims.quote: The ability to incur authorization failures refills at a rate of 1 per identifier every 12 minutes.
claims.claim: The refill rate for failed authorizations is 1 every 12 minutes.

claims.quote: Exceeding the Failed Validations limit is reported with the error message too many failed authorizations recently.
claims.claim: The error message for exceeding the hourly failure limit is "too many failed authorizations recently".

claims.quote: Up to 1,152 consecutive authorization failures per identifier can be incurred by one account.
claims.claim: The limit for consecutive authorization failures is 1,152 per identifier per account.

claims.quote: Once exceeded, the account is prevented from requesting new certificates for that identifier. Each time the subscriber attempts to request a certificate they will receive an error containing a link to our Self-Service Portal where they can unpause issuance for the paused identifier...
claims.claim: Exceeding the consecutive failure limit pauses issuance for the identifier, requiring manual unpausing via the Self-Service Portal.

claims.quote: Revoking certificates does not reset rate limits, because the resources used to issue those certificates have already been consumed.
claims.claim: Revoking certificates does not reset rate limits.

claims.quote: If you’ve hit a rate limit, we don’t have a way to temporarily reset it. Don’t worry, your capacity for that limit will gradually refill over time, allowing you to make more requests without any additional action on your part.
claims.claim: There is no manual way to reset rate limits; they refill automatically over time.

reported: Floating-point accumulation bug: self.tokens = self.tokens + ... can lead to the token count drifting slightly above self.capacity over many small, rapid calls. Because _refill doesn't cap the new token count at capacity, a user who makes many requests when the bucket is nearly full can accumulate more burst allowance than intended. It should be self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + elapsed  self.rate).

Race condition (Time-of-check to time-of-use): The check if key not in self.buckets and the subsequent assignment self.buckets[key] = ... are not atomic. If two threads call allow() with the same new key concurrently, both will see the key is missing, both will instantiate a new TokenBucket, and one will overwrite the other. This results in one thread getting a fresh bucket (effectively bypassing the limit for that initial request) and the other operating on a bucket that immediately gets replaced.

Logic defect in idle calculation: b.updated (from self.updated in TokenBucket) is always reset to now during _refill(), which is called every time try_acquire is called (line 25). This means now - b.updated measures the time since the last request, not the time since the bucket was actually full. A bucket that has been steadily draining but never completely empty (because requests keep coming in) will never be considered "idle," even if its token count is near zero. This prevents forget_idle from reclaiming memory for persistently active-but-low-volume keys.
